competitors.inventedNote: These three companies are invented for this demonstration. No data was gathered about any real business. Everything below is authored fixture content shaped like what genuine public observation would produce.
competitors.methodNote: The comparison table holds only things a person could confirm by opening a competitor website. That is a deliberate limit rather than a shortcoming: it is also the part of this workspace that tells you something you can act on.

subject.name: Summit & Sage Home Services
subject.positioning: Positions on diagnosis quality and honest advice. Strong decision-guide content, no published pricing.

competitors.name: Mile High Mechanical
competitors.positioning: Positions on speed and coverage: same-day service, named neighbourhoods, licensing detail on every technician page.
competitors.reasonTracked: Named in more recorded AI answers than any other Denver company, and publishes the pricing content Summit & Sage does not. The closest direct peer.

estimates.method: Modelled from positions observed on the 40 tracked queries multiplied by a published click-through curve. A model of a sample, not a measurement.

competitors.name: Front Range Comfort
competitors.positioning: Positions on price transparency: a published rate card and flat-fee diagnostics on the homepage.
competitors.reasonTracked: The tracked competitor whose pricing page assistants cite when answering cost questions, which is the prompt Summit & Sage stopped appearing in.

estimates.method: Modelled from positions observed on the 40 tracked queries multiplied by a published click-through curve. A model of a sample, not a measurement.

competitors.name: Cherry Creek Heating
competitors.positioning: Positions on premium installation and long warranties. Little service-repair content of any kind.
competitors.reasonTracked: Overlaps on replacement work rather than repair. Tracked to watch whether that boundary holds, not because the two compete week to week.

estimates.method: Modelled from positions observed on the 40 tracked queries multiplied by a published click-through curve. The band is proportionally widest here because the site ranks for fewest of them.

signals.question: Publishes price ranges for common repairs
signals.whyItMatters: Pricing questions are where a customer decides whether to call anyone. A site that answers them can be cited by an assistant; a site that does not cannot.

signals.question: Publishes a repair-or-replace decision guide
signals.whyItMatters: The strongest organic page Summit & Sage owns. No tracked competitor publishes an equivalent.

signals.question: States emergency availability on the homepage
signals.whyItMatters: The highest-intent visitors arrive already in trouble and leave if they cannot see whether anyone will come out tonight.

signals.question: Lists named service areas rather than a metro-wide claim
signals.whyItMatters: Named neighbourhoods are what a local query matches against and what an assistant repeats when asked for someone nearby.

signals.question: Publishes technician licensing and certification detail
signals.whyItMatters: Cited by assistants summarising trustworthiness, and one of the few claims a small business can make that a national aggregator cannot.

signals.question: Offers online booking rather than phone only
signals.whyItMatters: Relevant to the booking-rate divergence on the AC repair page: a competitor with a shorter path to a confirmed appointment is a competing explanation worth ruling out.

signals.question: Published anything in the last 90 days
signals.whyItMatters: Publishing cadence is visible from post dates and is the cheapest read available on whether anyone is actively working on the site.

competitors.overlapNote: Observed by running each query by hand from a Denver location in a clean browser profile on 3 August 2026. Search results are personalised and change through the day, so this is a snapshot of six queries at one moment, not a ranking report.

unavailable.metric: Their sessions, visitors or page views
unavailable.reason: Analytics data is private to whoever owns the property. Third-party traffic figures are models built from panel and clickstream sampling, and their error on a single small local business is large enough to reverse a comparison.

unavailable.metric: Their conversion rate or booking count
unavailable.reason: A conversion is an event inside somebody else’s analytics. Nothing observable from outside distinguishes a visitor who booked from one who left.

unavailable.metric: Their revenue or average job value
unavailable.reason: Not published by a private company and not derivable from anything visible. A figure here would be invention with a currency symbol attached.
Ad transparency tools show that ads ran, not what was paid. Spend estimates multiply guessed impressions by guessed rates.
Only the queries on the tracked list were checked, by hand, once. A complete footprint would require continuous crawling at a scale nothing here does.
